facts.fact_text: Mr I. Lutsenko took an active part in the Maidan protests.
On 22 December 2013, the council of the Maidan People's Union gave Mr I. Lutsenko the position of deputy chief supervisor in charge of order within the protesters' camp on Maidan Nezalezhnosti.

In his capacity as deputy chief supervisor in charge of order within the protesters' camp on Maidan Nezalezhnosti, Mr I. Lutsenko helped to take care of wounded protesters by transporting them to various medical facilities.
In January 2014, Mr Y. Verbytskyy came to Kyiv and took part in the Maidan protests.

According to a copy of a police record submitted by the Government, at 4.33 a.m. on 21 January 2014 a doctor from the hospital informed the police that Mr I. Lutsenko and Mr Y. Verbytskyy had been abducted from the hospital by several persons in plain clothes.
According to the relevant investigation files, the abductors used force against Mr I. Lutsenko and Mr Y. Verbytskyy.
The first applicant, Mr I. Lutsenko, was kicked in the face by the abductors, and consequently two of his teeth were broken.
Mr I. Lutsenko and Mr Y. Verbytskyy were placed in a vehicle by the abductors and taken to a remote area.
Mr I. Lutsenko and Mr Y. Verbytskyy were beaten and ill-treated by the abductors in a remote area.
On 21 January 2014, the outside temperature in Kyiv was around -10°C.
According to information provided by the first applicant and information contained in the investigation files, Mr I. Lutsenko and Mr Y. Verbytskyy were taken to a garage after being abducted.
In the garage, Mr I. Lutsenko and Mr Y. Verbytskyy were questioned by unidentified Russian-speaking individuals about their involvement in the Maidan protests.
During the questioning in the garage, Mr I. Lutsenko answered the questions in Russian.
During the questioning in the garage, Mr Y. Verbytskyy answered the questions in Ukrainian.
During the questioning in the garage, both Mr I. Lutsenko and Mr Y. Verbytskyy were subjected to repeated beatings and other forms of ill-treatment over the course of several hours.
The abductors put a plastic bag over Mr I. Lutsenko's head and tied it with duct tape.
A small hole was made in the plastic bag placed over Mr I. Lutsenko's head so that he could breathe.
The abductors tied Mr I. Lutsenko's hands and legs with duct tape and put him on the floor.
While Mr I. Lutsenko was lying on his left side, the abductors repeatedly kicked and punched him in the face, head, back, thighs, ankles and hands, particularly aiming to hit his joints.
Mr I. Lutsenko was beaten with wooden and metal sticks by the abductors.
During the beating, Mr I. Lutsenko was threatened with death on a number of occasions.

According to a forensic medical report dated 20 February 2014, established by an expert hired by the State, Mr I. Lutsenko had numerous haematomas and contusions on the trunk of his body, limbs, head and face.
The forensic medical report dated 20 February 2014 classified Mr I. Lutsenko's injuries as minor.
At about 4.30 a.m. on 21 January 2014, a doctor from the hospital informed the police of the abduction of Mr I. Lutsenko and Mr Y. Verbytskyy.
At about 9.30 a.m. on 21 January 2014, Mr I. Lutsenko's partner lodged a complaint with the police regarding his disappearance.
At about 6 p.m. on 21 January 2014, Mr I. Lutsenko was taken to a public road near a village in the Boryspil District, about 50 kilometres away from central Kyiv, and was left there.
From the public road near a village in the Boryspil District, Mr I. Lutsenko managed to get help.
Subsequently after being left on the public road, Mr I. Lutsenko was questioned by a police officer concerning the events of his abduction and ill-treatment.
Mr Y. Verbytskyy's wife lodged a complaint with the police regarding his abduction.
On 21 January 2014, a criminal investigation was launched into Mr Y. Verbytskyy's wife's complaint regarding his abduction.
On 22 January 2014, Mr Y. Verbytskyy's body was found in a forest in the Boryspil District.
A preliminary medical report recorded that Mr Y. Verbytskyy had died of hypothermia.
Multiple injuries were found on the trunk of Mr Y. Verbytskyy's body, limbs, head and face.

According to a forensic medical report of 12 March 2014, a copy of which was submitted to the Court, Mr Y. Verbytskyy's injuries included numerous haematomas all over the trunk of his body, limbs, head and face.
According to the forensic medical report of 12 March 2014, Mr Y. Verbytskyy's injuries included fractured bones and ribs.
According to the forensic medical report of 12 March 2014, Mr Y. Verbytskyy's injuries included internal bleeding.
According to the forensic medical report of 12 March 2014, it was considered that Mr Y. Verbytskyy had been hit by blunt objects at least thirty times.
The forensic medical report of 12 March 2014 confirmed that Mr Y. Verbytskyy had died of hypothermia.
On 22 January 2014, the police started a criminal investigation into the death of Mr Y. Verbytskyy, which was classified as murder.
The criminal investigation into Mr Y. Verbytskyy's abduction was joined to the criminal investigation into his death.
The second applicant took part in the criminal proceedings into Mr Y. Verbytskyy's death as a victim.
The second applicant was questioned regarding the events surrounding Mr Y. Verbytskyy's abduction and death.
The second applicant took part in other investigative actions in the criminal proceedings into Mr Y. Verbytskyy's death.
On 22 January 2014, the police started a criminal investigation into the first applicant Mr I. Lutsenko's abduction.
The criminal investigation into Mr I. Lutsenko's abduction was eventually merged with the investigation into the murder of Mr Y. Verbytskyy.
On 27 January 2014, Mr I. Lutsenko was questioned by the police about the events of his abduction and ill-treatment.

Mr I. Lutsenko stated that while he had been in the hands of his abductors, he had heard Mr Y. Verbytskyy being beaten more severely after the abductors had found out that he was originally from Lviv.
Mr I. Lutsenko stated that those beating Mr Y. Verbytskyy had repeatedly called him 'banderovets' (бандеровець).
Mr I. Lutsenko stated that he heard the abductors discussing the possibility of taking him and Mr Y. Verbytskyy to a police station.

According to the case material, including letters from the Prosecutor General's Office and the Ministry of Internal Affairs dated 4 February, 19 May, 15 June and 29 November 2016, between February and April 2014 thirteen individuals were identified as suspects in the investigation into the abduction and killing of Mr I. Lutsenko and Mr Y. Verbytskyy.
Two of the thirteen suspects, identified as T. and M., were suspected of having taken part in the abduction of Mr I. Lutsenko and Mr Y. Verbytskyy.
T. and M. were alleged to have been the drivers of the vehicles used in the abduction of Mr I. Lutsenko and Mr Y. Verbytskyy.

According to official notifications of suspicion issued by investigators from the Chief Investigative Department of the Ministry of Internal Affairs on 24 July 2014 informing T. that he was under suspicion, Mr I. Lutsenko's and Mr Y. Verbytskyy's abduction and ill-treatment were part of the authorities' attempt to suppress the Maidan protests.

According to official notifications of suspicion issued by investigators from the Chief Investigative Department of the Ministry of Internal Affairs on 28 July 2014 informing M. that he was under suspicion, Mr I. Lutsenko's and Mr Y. Verbytskyy's abduction and ill-treatment were part of the authorities' attempt to suppress the Maidan protests.

According to the official notifications of suspicion, different private individuals, including those with a criminal background, had been hired by unidentified law-enforcement officials to attack and intimidate the Maidan protesters.

According to the official notifications of suspicion, the group of suspects who had allegedly abducted and tortured Mr I. Lutsenko and Mr Y. Verbytskyy had been organised and directed by N., Ch. and Z.
According to the official notifications of suspicion, N., Ch. and Z. had acted on the instructions of unidentified representatives of State bodies.
According to the official notifications of suspicion, a number of other unidentified individuals were said to have participated in the ill-treatment of Mr I. Lutsenko and Mr Y. Verbytskyy.

According to the official notifications of suspicion, having tortured Mr Y. Verbytskyy in the garage and discovered that he was from Lviv, the suspects and other unknown individuals took him to an isolated forest.
According to the official notifications of suspicion, the suspects and other unknown individuals beat Mr Y. Verbytskyy in the isolated forest with the aim of killing him.

According to the official notifications of suspicion, the suspects considered Mr Y. Verbytskyy to be 'a representative of the most radical part of Western Ukraine, rallying against the ruling party and senior government officials.'
According to the official notifications of suspicion, the suspects left Mr Y. Verbytskyy in the forest, exposed to freezing temperatures, without any outer clothing.
According to the official notifications of suspicion, the suspects knew that Mr Y. Verbytskyy could not leave the forest area by himself because of his injuries.

According to the official notifications of suspicion, it was concluded that the suspects had assumed that Mr Y. Verbytskyy would die in the conditions in which he was left and that they had wanted him to die in this way.
According to the official notifications of suspicion, Mr Y. Verbytskyy's death was classified as murder.

According to the official notifications of suspicion, a forensic medical report of 3 February 2014 found that, because of his injuries, Mr Y. Verbytskyy had not been able to move freely, which had increased the negative consequences of his exposure to freezing temperatures, ultimately resulting in his death.
The trial of M. has been ongoing before the Pecherskyy District Court in Kyiv since June 2015.
Proceedings concerning the remaining twelve suspects, including T., were suspended because their whereabouts were unknown.
The twelve suspects whose proceedings were suspended were put on a wanted list.
According to the Ministry of Internal Affairs' letter of 29 November 2016, one of the suspects was located in Russia, but his extradition was refused by the Russian authorities.
The whereabouts of the other suspects who absconded were unknown.

According to the Government, in the course of the investigations into Mr I. Lutsenko's and Mr Y. Verbytskyy's abduction and the latter's murder, over 100 witnesses, suspects and victims were questioned.
According to the Government, in the course of the investigations into Mr I. Lutsenko's and Mr Y. Verbytskyy's abduction and the latter's murder, searches and forensic examinations were performed.
According to the Government, the first applicant Mr I. Lutsenko took an active part in the investigations and made no complaints at domestic level regarding their effectiveness.

The Government stated that no further details about the investigations could be provided because this could harm the investigations which were still ongoing, without giving any further information or explanation in that regard.

In the course of the investigations into the abduction and ill-treatment of Mr I. Lutsenko and Mr Y. Verbytskyy and the latter's murder, it was established that between 12 and 28 January 2014 Mr I. Lutsenko's telephone conversations had been intercepted by the police as part of an investigation in another case relating to the Maidan protests.

According to a copy of the extract from the official Ukrainian electronic database of criminal proceedings provided by the applicants, the investigators found evidence demonstrating that during the commission of the crimes against Mr I. Lutsenko and Mr Y. Verbytskyy the organisers of those crimes maintained permanent contact with the leadership of the Ministry of Internal Affairs.

According to a copy of the extract from the official Ukrainian electronic database of criminal proceedings provided by the applicants, the investigators found evidence that unidentified police officers shared with the organisers of the abduction of the protesters information concerning Mr I. Lutsenko's telephone conversations and location, which had been obtained in the course of police surveillance operations.
On 20 August 2014, the police launched a separate investigation into the possible involvement of agents of the police in the crimes committed against Mr I. Lutsenko and Mr Y. Verbytskyy.

According to a letter from the Prosecutor General's Office of 25 November 2016, on an unspecified date two police officers were charged with the unlawful interception of Mr I. Lutsenko's telephone conversations under Article 163 of the Criminal Code.

According to a letter from the Prosecutor General's Office of 25 November 2016, on an unspecified date two police officers were charged with falsification of official documents under Article 366 § 1 of the Criminal Code.

The case against the two police officers charged with unlawful interception of Mr I. Lutsenko's telephone conversations and falsification of official documents was referred to the Shevchenkivskyy District Court for trial.

According to information published on the Prosecutor General's Office's dedicated website, the proceedings before the Shevchenkivskyy District Court were not concluded at the time of the adoption of this judgment.

According to information published on the Prosecutor General's Office's dedicated website, the relevant proceedings into the crimes against Mr I. Lutsenko and Mr Y. Verbytskyy were ongoing at the time of the adoption of this judgment.

In March 2014, under the Act on State Support for the Victim Participants in Mass Actions of Civil Protest and their Family Members of 21 February 2014, the State Treasury paid the relatives of Mr Y. Verbytskyy a sum forming part of a total of UAH 243,600 on account of his death.

In February 2015, under the Act on State Support for the Victim Participants in Mass Actions of Civil Protest and their Family Members of 21 February 2014, the State Treasury paid the relatives of Mr Y. Verbytskyy a sum forming part of a total of UAH 243,600 on account of his death.
The total amount of UAH 243,600 paid by the State Treasury to the relatives of Mr Y. Verbytskyy was the equivalent of about EUR 13,300 at the material time.

Summaries of and extracts from the domestic legal framework and international reports of relevance for the examination of all applications lodged in relation to the Maidan protests and their aftermath, including the present two applications, are to be found in Shmorgunov and Others v. Ukraine.

Some of the international reports summarised in Shmorgunov and Others v. Ukraine also contain information relating specifically to the events at issue in the present case concerning Mr I. Lutsenko and Mr Y. Verbytskyy.
In its 2015 report, the International Advisory Panel made observations concerning the investigations relating to Mr I. Lutsenko and Mr Y. Verbytskyy.

According to the International Advisory Panel's 2015 report, 13 suspects, most of them titushky, as well as individuals identified as Zubrytskyi and Chebotariov, were served with notices of suspicion on various charges related to the incidents involving Mr I. Lutsenko and Mr Y. Verbytskyy.

According to the International Advisory Panel's 2015 report, two suspects were arrested, notified of suspicion and detained in connection with the incidents involving Mr I. Lutsenko and Mr Y. Verbytskyy.
According to the International Advisory Panel's 2015 report, on 20 August 2014 the indictments against the two arrested suspects were submitted to the court.
According to the International Advisory Panel's 2015 report, on 16 October 2014 the trial court returned the indictments against the two arrested suspects, citing certain shortcomings in them.

According to the International Advisory Panel's 2015 report, the prosecutor's appeal against the return of the indictments was due to be heard on 12 December 2014, and the International Advisory Panel had not been informed of the outcome of the appeal.

According to the International Advisory Panel's 2015 report, the proceedings concerning the remaining 11 suspects in the case involving Mr I. Lutsenko and Mr Y. Verbytskyy were suspended, with ten suspects on the wanted list and the eleventh being pursued through international co-operation arrangements.
The United Nations Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine published a Briefing Note on Accountability for Killings and Violent Deaths During the Maidan Protest in February 2019.

According to the United Nations Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine's February 2019 Briefing Note, all victims from the Maidan protests died or sustained lethal injuries in January-February 2014, when the protests turned violent following the adoption by Parliament of a series of laws that limited freedom of peaceful assembly and expression, and introduced criminal responsibility for extremism and the seizure of administrative buildings.

According to the United Nations Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine's February 2019 Briefing Note, the internal troops of the Ministry of Internal Affairs and Berkut special riot police units, who had been dispatched to restrain the protestors, were reinforced with civilian counter-protestors, so-called 'titushky', allegedly upon coordination with former senior police officials.

According to the United Nations Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine's February 2019 Briefing Note, the internal troops of the Ministry of Internal Affairs were disbanded and reformed into the National Guard.

According to the United Nations Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine's February 2019 Briefing Note, the Berkut special riot police units were disbanded shortly after the end of the Maidan protests and reformed into special units within regional police departments.

According to the United Nations Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine's February 2019 Briefing Note, five years after the end of the Maidan protests, accountability for the killings and violent deaths of 84 protestors, a man who did not participate in the protests, and 13 law enforcement officers had yet to be achieved.

According to the United Nations Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine's February 2019 Briefing Note, the investigation into the killing of 17 protestors and 13 law enforcement officers had still to identify individual perpetrators.
According to the United Nations Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine's February 2019 Briefing Note, only one person had been found guilty of unintentional killing of a protestor.

According to the United Nations Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine's February 2019 Briefing Note, two persons were found guilty of hooliganism in relation to an incident that resulted in the killing of another protestor.

According to the United Nations Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine's February 2019 Briefing Note, the Special Investigations Department identified 14 members of a 'titushky' group as being involved in the abduction, torture and killing of Mr Y. Verbytskyy.

According to the United Nations Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine's February 2019 Briefing Note, as of February 2019, 12 of the 14 identified members of the 'titushky' group involved in the abduction, torture and killing of Mr Y. Verbytskyy had absconded.

According to the United Nations Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine's February 2019 Briefing Note, on 23 April 2014, police detained two male members of the 'titushky' group involved in the abduction, torture and killing of Mr Y. Verbytskyy.

According to the United Nations Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine's February 2019 Briefing Note, the first of the two detained men owned a garage in the outskirts of Kyiv where both Mr I. Lutsenko and Mr Y. Verbytskyy were tortured and interrogated.

According to the United Nations Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine's February 2019 Briefing Note, the first detained man absconded shortly after being indicted on charges of abduction, torture and intentional killing.

According to the United Nations Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine's February 2019 Briefing Note, the second detained man, who acted as a lookout, was on trial facing abduction charges as of February 2019.

According to the United Nations Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine's February 2019 Briefing Note, on 17 July 2018, after almost three years of hearings on the merits of the case against the second detained man, the judge recused herself from the case.

According to the United Nations Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine's February 2019 Briefing Note, as of February 2019, a new judge in the case against the second detained man had still to be appointed.

According to the United Nations Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine's February 2019 Briefing Note, on 28 July 2017, Special Investigations Department investigators detained another member of the 'titushky' group on charges of the creation of a criminal organisation, interference with public assemblies, abduction, torture and intentional killing of Mr Y. Verbytskyy.

According to the United Nations Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine's February 2019 Briefing Note, on 24 July 2018, the third detained member of the 'titushky' group was indicted and his case was sent for trial.

According to the United Nations Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine's February 2019 Briefing Note, as of February 2019, the third detained defendant remained in detention while the court heard testimonies of prosecution witnesses, including other members of 'titushky' groups.

According to the United Nations Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine's February 2019 Briefing Note, the Department for Organised Crime Investigation indicted two police officers for unlawful surveillance over Mr I. Lutsenko, who was abducted together with Mr Y. Verbytskyy during the Maidan protests.

According to the United Nations Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine's February 2019 Briefing Note, the criminal proceeding into the organisation of unlawful surveillance of Mr I. Lutsenko was merged with the case of abduction, torture and killing of Mr Y. Verbytskyy.

According to the United Nations Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine's February 2019 Briefing Note, the prosecution for the killing of Mr Y. Verbytskyy was marred by the failure of the Government to ensure the appearance at court of one of the key defendants.

According to the United Nations Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine's February 2019 Briefing Note, the failure to ensure the trial without undue delay of the second member of the 'titushky' group was also a concern.
